characters.name: Moss
characters.backstory:
Moss builds it his way. He has been told, by the guild, by the grange and once in writing by the Capital City, that the way is on the sheet; and Moss reads the sheet, puts it down, and does the thing that works. It has cost him two commissions and a formal warning and it has also given the borough a plough hitch that does not foul, a bridge arch a third lighter than the drawing, and a bench jig half the workshop now uses without knowing whose it was.

He is not a difficult animal about it, which is the confusing part. He is cheerful, he turns up, he takes the apprentice nobody else wants, and then he quietly builds it the other way and lets the result argue. About a third of the time the result loses and Moss rebuilds it properly and says so. The Town Workshop has stopped sending anybody to check.

Berry walked him through his first joint when he was twelve and has been the one animal Moss will listen to about anything ever since. What Berry actually taught him, Moss will tell you, was not the joint — it was that you work it out yourself, which is exactly what the guild now finds so annoying.
characters.voice: Easy, unbothered, already doing it. 'Yeah, that's the drawing. Watch this.'
characters.arc: Moss makes the town cheaper to build and harder to knock over, and he never once does it the way the sheet says. The Ploughwright (1) braces the borough. The Toolsmith (2) works a shift and the next Building comes in under the drawing. The Guild Architect (3) picks an animal back up out of Unemployment cheap. The Rocketwright (4) is Moss and Comet arguing productively. The Bridgewright (5) is the arch that should not stand: he is busy, and one of your Characters is on its feet because of what he worked out. Added since: a Timber Hand at 0 with no ability — Moss at eleven, before Berry got hold of him.

characters.name: Daniel
characters.backstory:
Daniel draws the maps and does not go. They have charted the canal from the ferry steps to the county line, the roads out past the toll gate, the coast they have never smelled and, on clear nights from a window, the stars; and the furthest they have been from the borough in their life is the far hedgerow, once, with somebody else.

It is not that they do not want to. It is that they want to enormously, in the abstract, from a desk, with the door shut. A map is the whole adventure with none of the going: the routes, the distances, the marginal note about where the bank shelves and which inn will take a mouse after dark, all of it true and all of it happening to somebody else. Traders come back from the Capital City road and Daniel debriefs them for two hours, corrects the chart, rolls it up, and sleeps in their own bed.

The borough gets a great deal out of this. Everything Brooke's lightermen run by, everything the Science hall's surveys are laid over, and every apprentice sent out to somewhere they have never been with a sheet in their paw and a mouse's careful handwriting on it — all Daniel's, and every one of those animals has been somewhere Daniel has not.
characters.voice: Soft, exact, endlessly curious about elsewhere. 'And what was it like, past the second lock? No — tell me properly.'
characters.arc: Daniel's cards are the route known before the journey: the Event costs one animal fewer, and the top of the deck arrives in the order they charted. Ink Mixer (0) is the desk and the discount. Canal Cartographer (2) adds the chart itself. Star Charter (3) is the window and the night sky, and takes a Character off the Event while they are working. Master Cartographer (4) is the whole wall of maps — the deck in the order they want and a look at what the Capital City is bringing out next, which is as close as Daniel gets to leaving. Added since: a Chart Copier at 1 with no ability — the tracing itself, which has no decisions in it.

characters.name: Ned
characters.backstory:
Ned keeps the record, and the record is right. Every ward roll, every guild return, every date the bridge was out and every name on the hiring list since before Ned was born — filed, cross-referenced and correct, because a record that is nearly correct is a record that will one day be quoted by somebody who is nearly wrong.

They are by the book in the literal sense: the book exists, Ned wrote most of the current edition of it, and they will hand it to you open at the page rather than paraphrase. This makes them unpopular in a meeting and indispensable the following week. The borough's two standing arguments about the far hedgerow were both settled out of Ned's shelves in an afternoon, which is the kind of thing that stops being annoying the moment it is your argument.

What nobody sees is the putting by. A Squirrel archivist does not spend the find — Ned notices a discrepancy, files it, and says nothing for a year, and then the whole thing comes out at once, in order, with the dates. Lynnette prints what Ned certifies and has never had to print a correction.
characters.voice: Level, careful, allergic to 'roughly'. Says 'that is close, and it is not what happened'.
characters.arc: Ned files, and then Ned opens the file. The Page Runner (1) puts Supply by on every shift, the Squirrel's own slow start. The Night Archivist (2) sets the top of the deck in order. The Reference Librarian (4) does both — the order and another coin put by. The Chancellor of Records (5) is the year of quiet filing paid out in one go: every coin the town has put by, taken in at once, on the record. Added since: a Ward Recorder at 3 who draws off the turn's first Civics Event — the shelf opening on the ward's business.

characters.name: Daisy
characters.backstory:
Daisy is the borough's florist and a hopeless romantic in the full, unembarrassed sense of the word. She knows every scent in the hedgerow by name, she can tell you what a posy is saying and what the animal who ordered it thinks it is saying, and she has sold flowers to most of the couples in the First Boroughs at one end of things or the other.

Her own life is entirely ahead of her. Daisy is waiting to be swept off her feet — properly, without warning, by somebody who turns up at the stall and means it — and she has been waiting cheerfully for years, which the borough finds either lovely or maddening depending on who you ask. In the meantime she sweeps the petals up at the end of the day and dries them, because a Squirrel does not throw away anything that will keep, and the night-bloom stock and the wedding trade and the Festival Green garlands all come out of what she put by in the quiet months.

Festival week is hers. Every garland on the square, every buttonhole in the hall, four days of no sleep, and a full year's takings in one go — which is exactly how a Squirrel likes to be paid.
characters.voice: Bright, dreamy, faster than you expect. 'Don't tell me — no, don't — is it for her?'
characters.arc: Everything Daisy does is put by now and spent all at once later. The Petal Sweeper (0) dries what falls. The Bouquet Weaver (2) looks three cards down the deck for the one she is hoping for. The Night-Bloom Florist (3) works the dark and puts by double. The Festival Florist (4) is the week itself: four days of garlands, and every coin the whole town has stored taken in at the end of it.

wantedVerbs.verb: pairCharacters (two Characters in a town who are worth more to each other)
wantedVerbs.why: Daisy's whole story is the sweeping-off-her-feet that has not happened yet, and the card wanted to notice the animal she is standing next to.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Left as the Squirrel's storage thread — she puts by, and the Festival pays out — with the romance carried in the flavor. `otherCharacterInTown` can name one animal, but Daisy does not know who it is yet, which is the point of her.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `pairCharacters`: Daisy and one other animal are worth 1 more to each other on every shift either of them works, for as long as both keep standing in the town. The bond is read back through the partner rather than promised, so it lapses on its own the moment one of them is unemployed, upgraded away or sent home — which is the other half of the sweeping-off-her-feet that has not happened yet.

characters.name: Peter
characters.backstory:
Peter lays hedges. He was born at the far end of the borough within sight of the far hedgerow and has spent his working life inside it: cutting the stems most of the way through, bending them over while they are still living, pegging them down and letting them grow back into a wall. It takes a winter to do a field's length and about fifteen years to find out whether you did it properly.

This is why the borough's hedges are harder to take down than they look. Maribel files the objection at the meeting; Peter is the reason there is still something there to object about. The two of them have never discussed it.
characters.voice: Slow, practical, mostly about the hedge. Answers a question about himself with an answer about the hedge.
characters.arc: Two rungs and no tricks at all, which is the maker's brief for him: the lad with the billhook at 0, and the hedgelayer whose winter's work will still be standing in fifteen years at 3. The long shift is the whole of the second card — a hedge is not laid in a turn, and Peter is paid for what is there at the end of it.

characters.name: Osh
characters.backstory:
Osh goes round the borough with a treadle wheel on a handcart and puts an edge back on things. Knives, shears, billhooks, the mill's dressing picks, the bakery's scrapers, one ceremonial sword that has never cut anything. He does a circuit that takes eleven days and has done it in the same order since he was small enough to need a box to stand on.

He is a mouse and the wheel is nearly as big as he is, which the borough finds funnier than he does. Morty's mill kitchen and Marmalade's bakery are both on day four.
characters.voice: Quiet, exact, and briefly unbearable about other animals' edges.
characters.arc: Two rungs, both of them the wheel. At 0 he is on somebody else's round; at 2 it is his round, his order and his eleven days, which is why the second card works the long shift for more.

characters.name: Adam
characters.backstory:
Adam mends roads. The lane down to the ferry steps, the long pull up to the county gate, the square's cobbles after festival week — all of it is his, and all of it is work nobody notices until it stops being done. He was out on the county road the year the bridge went, and stayed out on it for most of that spring getting carts round the long way.

He is a Badger about it in the ordinary Badger fashion: he starts at one end, he does not hurry, and he is still there at the end of the day when everybody who came to watch has gone home.
characters.voice: Level and unhurried. Talks about a road the way other animals talk about a relative.
characters.arc: The lad with the barrow at 1 and the animal who decides where the road goes at 4. Both cards do nothing but work, because a road is nothing but work; the difference between them is how much of it is his.

characters.name: Cassadee
characters.backstory:
Open mic nights in the First Boroughs happen in whatever room will have them, and Cassadee is the animal who decides which room. She books it, sweeps it, sets the chairs, finds the lamp oil, stands at the back with the list, and puts the chairs away again at midnight. She does not sing, play, recite or juggle, and has turned down every invitation to try.

Oatmeal's band is on her list more often than anybody, which she says is because they turn up on time and not because there are five of them and four are brothers and sisters.
characters.voice: Brisk, kind, immovable about the running order. Says 'you are on at nine' as though it were a law.
characters.arc: Two rungs of the same evening: the animal carrying the chairs in at 0, and the animal whose room it is at 3. Nothing on either card but the work, which is the point — the show is somebody else's, and Cassadee is what it stands on.

characters.name: Annabelle
characters.backstory:
Everything the borough throws out goes through the Salvage Yard, and everything with words on it goes through Annabelle. She pulls the paper out before the weather gets at it: ward minutes, split almanacs, bills of lading, half a novel, the Grain Exchange's returns for a year nobody can otherwise account for. What is legible she flattens, dries and files. What is not she keeps anyway, on the grounds that she has been wrong before.

She and Beck have an arrangement of long standing and no written terms: she keeps the ones with words on, he gets first read of anything with a story in it, and neither of them has ever had to say so out loud.
characters.voice: Dry, unbothered, faintly amused at what animals throw away.
characters.arc: Paper Sorter (0) is the yard in the rain; Salvage Archivist (3) is the dry shed, the press and the shelves. Neither card does anything clever, because the work is the same work either way and the only thing that changes is how much of it survives.

characters.name: Liz
characters.backstory:
Liz keeps the weighbridge at the Grain Exchange. Every loaded cart in or out of the borough's biggest building crosses her plate, and what she writes on the docket is what everybody after her is paid on. Copper's office certifies the bridge every spring and has never once had to adjust it.

It is the job Finn had and lost, which the borough mentions to neither of them. Liz is a Fox and reads a carter's face while the beam is settling, and has never needed to do anything about what she reads there, because the beam settles where it settles.
characters.voice: Short, level, faintly bored. Reads the number out once.
characters.arc: Scale Hand (1) is the beam and somebody else's docket; Weighbridge Keeper (4) is the beam, the docket and the signature. A weighbridge does not need an ability: the whole of its power is that the number is the number.

characters.name: Taco
characters.backstory:
Taco cooks on a cart at the ferry steps and keeps the hours the river keeps, which is to say no hours at all. Lightermen come off a boat at four in the morning wanting something hot and Taco is there with it; the cart is shut at noon when everybody else's is busiest, and open again when the evening boats come down.

He is an Otter and cannot stand still, so the cart moves too — steps, Boat Shed, the top of the lane — and the river trade finds it anyway, every time, by a method nobody has ever explained to a landsman.
characters.voice: Fast, cheerful, several things at once. Asks how the run went before he asks what you want.
characters.arc: Cart Cook (1) is the pan and somebody else's cart; Quayside Cook (3) is his cart, his hours and the whole river trade's supper. Both do nothing but feed animals, which on the steps at four in the morning is the entire job.

characters.name: Cookie
characters.backstory:
Cookie bakes for the Winter Stores. Everything that comes off her board is made to keep: hard biscuit, twice-baked rusk, seed cake that improves for a month and is edible for a year. She uses the Community Oven like everybody else, on the late heat after the bread is out, which is the cool slow end nobody else wants and exactly the end she needs.

She is a Squirrel and the Winter Stores are the largest cache in the borough, so the arrangement was more or less inevitable. She has never eaten anything she baked in the year she baked it.
characters.voice: Practical, warm, slightly stern about dates. Gives you one and tells you not to open it yet.
characters.arc: Biscuit Maker (0) is the corner of somebody's board; Winter Stores Cook (3) is the whole late heat and the Stores' shelves behind it. Neither card does anything on the turn it lands, which is a fair description of Cookie's entire trade.

characters.name: Sota
characters.backstory:
Sota grinds glass. Every lens in the Observatory's smaller instruments came off their bench, and the two big ones have been re-seated by them twice. It is months of work to take a blank down to a figure that will hold a star still, and the last of it is done by hand, by feel, at about the speed of a plant growing.

They have been invited to look through the finished article on many occasions and have gone each time out of politeness. What Sota wants to know is whether the edge is right. What the star is doing is the Observatory's business.
characters.voice: Soft, unhurried, entirely uninterested in the sky.
characters.arc: Lens Grinder (1) is the bench and the blank; Telescope Fitter (3) is the bench, the tube and the cell it sits in. The work is months long and does nothing until it is finished, so neither card does anything either.

characters.name: Andrew
characters.backstory:
Andrew keeps the late desk at the Lending Library — the hours after the children's corner has emptied and the last of the evening readers have gone. He locks up after Inkwell's evening and does not go home. What cannot be lent out he copies by hand, a page or two a night, so that there is a second one.

He is an Owl, so the hours suit him and the pay does not. The library has never been able to explain the arrangement to the Counting House and has stopped trying.
characters.voice: Mild, unhurried, apologetic about the hour and plainly delighted by it.
characters.arc: Night Copyist (0) is one desk and one lamp; Keeper of the Late Desk (2) is the whole dark half of the building. An Owl earns almost nothing, and Andrew earns rather less than that, so both cards are small — which is the character, not an oversight.

characters.name: Orien
characters.backstory:
Orien counts things. He has counted things since he was small enough to be lifted onto the Counting House steps to wait for somebody, and he has never found a reason to stop. What the borough took a while to understand is that he is not doing it for anyone. He does it the way other animals whittle. He came home from his first week of paid work with a table of every price the Capital City had taken that season, drawn out in four colours, for nobody.

There is a machine in the back room of his house. He built it out of what the Observatory threw away and what Patch would sell him, and it has been rebuilt four times since; it clicks all evening and most of the night, and it is the reason he is never at the bonfire. Into it go the shift returns, the auction prices, the ferry's crossings, the weight of every cart Liz has ever put on her plate. Out of it come the tables the almanac prints — Lynnette sets them, Orien supplies them, and nobody in the borough has ever paid for a figure since. Ask him what a Building will go for and he will tell you, and he will be within a Supply, and he will be a little put out if you sound surprised.

He is not good with animals, which he knows, and which he has decided is a fair trade. He has been made a committee's figures badger eleven times and has never once been asked to speak. He likes it best when a meeting goes quiet and looks at him, and he can put a number on the table and go home.
characters.voice: Precise, cheerful, and a little too fast. Answers the question you should have asked. Says 'well — it depends what you mean by cheap' and then tells you, at length, what it depends on.
characters.arc: Five jobs, one habit: Orien changes what a thing costs. The Tally Clerk at 0 works out a cheaper way to hire the next animal and hands the note over. The Rate Checker at 2 has read the lot before you challenged it, so challenging is cheaper. The Borough Actuary at 3 prices the Capital City's Buildings a season ahead, and the town buys under the number. The Survey Computer at 4 is the machine at full tilt: every shift the town finishes that turn pays more than it should. The Town Planner at 5 is what all of it was for: he sits down with the whole borough's figures and the next animal through the door comes in well under budget.

characters.name: Patch
characters.backstory:
Patch went into the Salvage Yard as a kit because there was money in it if you were small enough to get under things and quick enough to get out again. That was the whole of the plan for about two years. Then he sold a mangle back to the animal who had thrown it away, for more than it had cost new, because he had put a new roller in it — and he understood, standing there with the coin in his paw, that the diving was the least interesting part of the business.

So he built the rest of it. He takes it out, he sorts it, he mends what is worth mending and improves what is worth improving, and he sells it back to the borough at a price nobody has ever complained about. Annabelle takes the paper — that is hers, and the two of them have never once discussed it — and Patch takes everything else. What he is really known for now is the judging. Animals bring him things and ask whether they are worth keeping, and he turns them over twice and tells them, and he is right. Word got round, and now they bring him other things to ask the same question about: a trade, a lease, a season that has not gone well, somebody they are not sure about. He turns those over twice as well.

He will tell you he is not qualified, which is true, and that he is only a raccoon with a yard, which is also true, and then he will tell you to keep the lease and sell the cart, and you will, and it will have been the right way round.
characters.voice: Unhurried, dry, entirely certain. Asks two questions and then gives you the answer. Says 'that's worth keeping' and 'that isn't, and you know it isn't' in exactly the same tone.
characters.arc: The business, built upward out of the bins. The Junkyard Diver at 0 is the kit under the pile, and every shift he works the town puts something up cheaper out of what he dragged home. The Salvage Sorter at 2 has a bench and a price list, so what the town raises next comes in cheaper. The Valuer at 3 is the job the borough actually made for him: he goes through the Dump and comes back with the thing and the reason. The Yard Foreman at 4 runs the whole yard, so every shift he finishes turns something discarded into something standing. The Reclamation Merchant at 5 is the far end of the mangle: he takes out of the Dump and puts up cheap, and the town's next Building is half somebody else's old one.

The town ends up with the better Building; it just cannot hand the old one back.

Both halves or neither, so a town with nothing up has nothing to trade and an empty Dump nothing to trade for. The old mangle out, the mended one in, and the Reclamation Merchant is the card that does it.

characters.name: Pebble
characters.backstory:
The crossing has been Pebble's family's for seven generations. Their father had it, and his father, and his grandmother before that, and her daughter after her, and the borough long ago stopped bothering with the names: whoever is on the boat is the ferryotter, and the ferryotter is whoever is on the boat. Most families with a thing like that behind them produce, sooner or later, somebody who wants out. Pebble's family has been waiting three generations for that animal and it is not going to be Pebble.

They like it. That is the whole of it, and it takes some animals a while to believe. Four crossings an hour, the same bank, the same rope, the same eleven regulars and their eleven opinions, and Pebble goes home at the end of it perfectly content. Brooke, who is climbing the ladder out of exactly this job toward the River Otter licence, has asked them about it directly, twice. Pebble said that standing where their father stood, doing what their father did, with his grandmother's fare chits still in the tin, is not a thing you climb out of. The chits are the other half of it: their family struck their own, a worn wooden otter on a round of hard wood, handed to every passenger and counted back at the far bank. Half the borough has one in a pocket that they never handed back, and the rest of the town's chits — the study marks, the building marks — are copies of the ferry's.

They are not ambitious and they are not bored, and both of those facts make the Harbourmaster's office slightly uneasy. Willow has offered Pebble the warden's post three times. Pebble took it on the third offer on the condition that it did not mean giving up the boat.
characters.voice: Easy, unhurried, entirely without edge. Talks about their great-grandmother in the present tense by accident. Says 'mind the step' about four hundred times a day and means it every time.
characters.arc: One job, four generations deep, and every rung hands out more of the family's chits. The Crossing Hand at 0 earns one a shift. The Bridge Courier at 1 hands one over with the fare and has somebody else up and moving by morning. The Ferry Master at 3 is the boat at full tempo — the shift slides from paw to paw, Otter-fashion, and a chit goes into the tin with it. The Harbour Warden at 5 is Willow's post, taken on the third asking and only on terms: a chit every turn, and once the tin is deep enough the crossing pays the town as well as the family.

wantedVerbs.why: The story wants a chit for every animal who crosses — a token per Character the town readies or moves, not a flat one per shift.
wantedVerbs.workaround: A fixed `gainToken` count on each version, rising with the rung. The tin fills at the same rate on a busy turn and a quiet one, which is the one thing a ferry never does.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `gainToken: { per: "charactersReadied" }`: a chit for every animal who actually crossed. `p.turn.readied` counts the Characters who have stood up in this town this turn — in the Ready phase or by any effect that put one back on its feet — and the Harbour Warden reads it at the end of the turn, when the count is what really happened. A busy turn fills the tin and a quiet one does not, which is the one thing a ferry never used to do.

characters.name: Scott
characters.backstory:
Scott writes it all down and then sells it back to the borough in pamphlets. Half of what comes off Lynnette's press with his name on it is invention — dragons under the far hedgerow, a lighterman who bargains with the river, the winter the moon came down for a look — and the other half is the plain truth about what the borough did in 1841, with the dates right. He does not keep the two apart on the shelf, and he will not be drawn on which sells better.

The rule he does keep is that the true half is true. Everything he writes about a real animal or a real year goes across Ned's shelves first, and Ned certifies it or Scott cuts it, and in fifteen years Lynnette has never had to print a correction to anything of his. It makes him slow. It also means that when Scott says the bridge went in a particular spring, the borough stops arguing about which spring. What it never makes him is dull: he has worked out, over a long career, exactly where in a ward-boundary dispute to put a joke about somebody's uncle, and exactly where in a reading for the little ones to put a fart.

He collects more than he prints. Every market between here and the Capital City, every lighterman coming off a night run, every old animal on a bench — he takes the story, pays for it with a better one, and puts it by. Most of it goes into the tin and stays there for years. When a season finally calls for it, he opens the tin, and it turns out he has had the answer since about a decade ago.
characters.voice: Warm, digressive, always three sentences from a joke. Starts things with 'now, this is the true one' and means it about half the time, on purpose.
characters.arc: Collect, print, verify, pay out — a Squirrel's shape, which is to say poor for a long time and then suddenly not. The Story Collector at 0 works the markets and puts everything by. The Pamphleteer at 2 is the press run: he sets the top of the deck the way he sets a page, and knows what is coming next. The Town Chronicler at 3 is the Ned years, slow and unarguable: he orders his own deck and watches the Capital City's at the same time. The Natural Historian at 4 goes out after the things nobody has written down yet and puts more by. The Author of the Boroughs at 5 opens the tin: a lifetime of collecting, cashed in at once, which is exactly what a Squirrel is for.

characters.name: Lindsay
characters.backstory:
Lindsay is not paying attention. She has not been paying attention for about twenty years and the glasshouse has never been better. She waters along the bench with the can held out at exactly the right height for exactly the right count, eyes somewhere past the roof glass, thinking about something that has nothing whatever to do with the roof glass, and every pot gets what it wants. Ask her afterwards what she did and she cannot tell you. Ask the pots and they can.

What she is thinking about is never quite established. She has been overheard costing out a glasshouse on the moon, working out how far a seed could fall, and settling an argument nobody was having about whether rain has a smell before or after it lands. The borough finds this restful. Rosabeth sings to her plants in full view and has done for thirty years; Lindsay does the opposite and gets the same result, and between the two of them the borough has stopped expecting gardening to make sense. The one place it shows up as a problem is a conversation: she will agree warmly with something you did not say and then ask you a question you already answered.

Her beds come in over. Always, every year, more than the row should give, and she cannot account for it and has stopped trying — she says the counting is somebody else's department and she is right, it is Orien's, and his figures on her glasshouse have a note in the margin that just says 'ask her again in spring'. Marmalade gets her rosemary and will not use anybody else's. Comet, who has been turned down twice by a selection board for wanting the moon too openly, likes her enormously.
characters.voice: Dreamy, kind, half a beat late. Trails off mid-sentence and comes back to it four minutes later, correctly. Says 'oh — sorry — yes' more than any other animal in the borough.
characters.arc: Five rungs of not paying attention, paying better and better. The Potting Helper at 0 finishes a shift and comes up with more than the row should give. The Glasshouse Hand at 2 keeps the whole growing side earning while there is another Agriculture animal about. The Herb Grower at 3 is the daydream itself: she is halfway through something else and does the work anyway, because it is second nature — the one time a Cat's own rules do not apply to her. The Conservatory Keeper at 4 has the benches producing over for everybody. The Moon Gardener at 5 is where her head has been the whole time, and the borough finally gets paid for it.

characters.name: Pockets
characters.backstory:
Pockets taught Patch to dive. That is the fact he leads with, and it is true, and it has been getting steadily less useful to him for about fifteen years. He was first into the Salvage Yard, first under the pile, first to work out which of the Capital City's carters would take a bent thing off you at the gate and ask nothing; and then his little brother put a new roller in a mangle, and built a business, and got a counter and a price list and a reputation for telling animals the truth about their leases, and Pockets did not.

What he got instead was range. There is nothing in the borough's dumps he cannot get back out and very little he cannot find a buyer for, including things the buyer should not have and things that were never anybody's to sell. He works the City Dump the way his brother works the yard, except that Patch sells you back your own mangle, mended, and Pockets sells you somebody else's, and does not say whose. Nothing he does is quite a crime. Several things he does are the shape of one, seen from a distance, in poor light.

The brothers are on speaking terms. Pockets turns up at the yard about four times a year, is fed, and leaves with something; Patch has never once asked what for, which is the nearest thing to forgiveness either of them goes in for. The borough hires Pockets when it wants a thing back that it has already thrown away, and is careful not to ask how, and pays him in the same careful way.
characters.voice: Quick, charming, all shoulders. Answers the question next to the one you asked. Says 'now I never said that' about things he has just said.
characters.arc: Three rungs, all of them the same trade at increasing nerve. The Kerbside Dealer at 1 gets an Event back out of your own Town Dump — small, legitimate, his brother's method. The Odd-Lot Dealer at 3 works the shared City Dump as well and comes back with both. The Salvage Raccoon at 4 is hired out of the Capital City by a town that wants something back and has decided not to ask how.

wantedArt.why: The Odd-Lot Dealer is a raccoon at the gate at dusk with a barrow under a sheet, dealing with a carter who is not getting down. neighbors/4 is the salvage portrait his brother already uses.

characters.name: Hibiscus
characters.backstory:
Hibiscus walks the borough's round. Juniper takes the post that leaves the borough and Hibiscus takes the post that stays in it, and the two of them hand over at the sorting bench every morning at five, which is the only part of the day Hibiscus does quickly. After that it is doors. Every door, in order, and at a fair number of them somebody comes out, and that is where the schedule goes.

They are not bad at the job. They are, by any measure the Hiring Hall keeps, extremely good at it: nothing is lost, nothing is misdelivered, and Hibiscus knows which house on which lane has somebody in it who has not been seen for three days, which is a thing no ledger in the borough records. It is simply that a round which ought to take four hours takes seven, because a bunny who genuinely wants to know how your mother is cannot be got off a doorstep in under ten minutes, and they genuinely want to know, at every door, every day. The borough has decided this is the arrangement. Complaints about the late second post are filed at the Hiring Hall next to the ones about the county gate and come to about as much.

What the round actually does is get the borough up. Hibiscus arrives, the door opens, somebody who was going to have a slow morning is now standing in it with their apron on and an opinion about the ferry, and by the time the round is done half the lane is out of doors and working. Biff walks his beat to stop trouble. Hibiscus walks theirs and the trouble never starts, which nobody has ever put in a report.
characters.voice: Bright, unhurried, endlessly interested. Opens with a question about somebody's family and gets the answer. Says 'no, go on' at the exact moment they should be leaving.
characters.arc: Five rungs of the same round, waking more of the town each time. The Post Runner at 1 gets one animal up for the morning. The Night Mail at 2 does it on the way home as well. The Round Walker at 3 turns a finished shift into somebody else's start. The Mail Coach Driver at 4 keeps the hour whether the passengers are aboard or not — the one job where Hibiscus is early — and has somebody up and waiting the moment the town announces anything. The Postmaster at 5 is the whole lane out of doors by nine: Hibiscus comes up, and an animal who was going to have a slow morning is standing in the doorway with their apron on.

characters.name: Quill
characters.backstory:
Quill's parents had the orchard and their parents had it before that, and Quill grew up in it — under it, mostly, in the long grass between the rows, being handed up windfalls. When it came to her she did not have to decide anything, which she is aware is a kind of luck other animals do not get. She could not imagine doing anything else and has never tried very hard to.

What she has decided, over and over, is that the orchard should be full. An orchard does not need thirty animals in it; hers has thirty animals in it anyway, most weekends, because she cannot bear the rows to be quiet. There is a cider social in the barn from September to about February and a bonfire whenever the prunings get above knee height, which is more often than pruning strictly requires. She invents reasons. Half the borough has picked for her one autumn, and about a third of them turned up for a Saturday and were still there at the end of the week, on the books, being paid.

That is the other thing the orchard does, and Quill will not be thanked for it. Rosabeth's garden takes the animals who have stopped getting up and mends them; the orchard takes everybody, all the time, whether or not anything is wrong, which means a hedgehog who is quietly out of work can be in the rows on Saturday morning without ever having admitted to anything. The Hiring Hall knows. It sends them. Quill pretends not to have noticed, hands them a basket, and puts the kettle on for thirty.
characters.voice: Loud, delighted, always catering for more animals than are present. Ends most sentences with 'come Saturday'. Never asks whether you are all right; asks whether you can carry a ladder.
characters.arc: The orchard, filling up. The Orchard Hand at 0 gets one animal into the rows where nothing can reach them. The Orchard Keeper at 2 is the standing rule of the place: nobody who is here loses their place here. The Cider Maker at 3 is the barn in September — the social pays, and somebody under the rafters is safe for the evening. The Orchard Scribe at 4 keeps the book of which tree fruited when, which is also the book of who picked, and the whole orchard holds while she is busy. The Harvest Steward at 5 is the season entire: the rows full, the books shut, and not one animal in them out of work.

wantedArt.why: The Cider Maker is the barn in September with the press going and thirty animals in it — a Food scene the orchard tiles (neighbors/9, the keeper among the trees) do not have.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_quill_cider_maker_3 → the nightskies atlas, tile 9. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Quinn
characters.backstory:
Quinn is at everything. The ward meeting, the boundary hearing, the reading of a will, the argument at the weighbridge, the bad meeting after the bridge went — Quinn was at the back of all of them with the book open, and Quinn said nothing at any of them. He has been the borough's scrivener for as long as anyone can produce a date for, which is itself a small joke, because if anybody could produce a date it would be him.

He is not unfriendly. He answers if you ask him something, in about four words, and then goes back to it. The trouble is that a great many animals have said something in a room he was in and watched his pen move, and it is an unsettling thing to be recorded by somebody who will not tell you what he made of it. Two or three of the older animals will not sit with their backs to him. The children, on the other hand, adore him: there is a settled belief among the borough's young that Quinn is a mage, on the grounds that the writing comes out faster than the talking goes in, and that he was seen at the fair, the regatta and the Hiring Hall on the same afternoon. Inkwell, who has a rumour of his own and has never denied it either, was asked once to settle it. Inkwell said only that Quinn writes faster than he does.

What the book is actually for is this. When a place falls vacant the Hiring Hall comes to Quinn, and Quinn turns back four years and finds the animal who did that exact work in a bad winter and has not been asked since, and writes the name on a slip, and hands it over, and says nothing. More animals in this borough have been got back into work by that slip than by any committee sitting.
characters.voice: Four words at most, and all four load-bearing. Writes while you are still talking. When he does speak it lands in a quiet room and is usually a date.
characters.arc: Three rungs, one book, pointed at Unemployment. The Meeting Scribe at 1 is at the back of the room, and a finished shift gets one animal back in cheap. The Town Scrivener at 3 is the post as the Capital City hires it, and the Mouse signature with it: whatever was written down comes back out of the Dump. The Keeper of the Record at 5 is the whole archive open: he turns back four years and the right name comes back for nothing.

wantedArt.why: The Keeper of the Record is the archive at night, one mouse and four years of shelving open at once. capital/4 is the Capital City's hiring portrait and is the job below it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_quinn_keeper_of_the_record_5 → the capital atlas, tile 4. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

characters.name: Roger
characters.backstory:
Roger can fix things. Not one kind of thing — the lock, the lease, the rota, the argument between the two carters, the reason the ward's accounts do not add up — and he does it without much fuss and usually on the way to somewhere else. The borough has noticed. The borough's response to noticing an animal like that is always the same, and Roger has been made chair, warden, clerk, judge and ombudsman of one thing or another since he was about twenty-two, every single time by a room turning round and looking at him.

He is bad at it. Not at the work — at the office. The job of a chair is to decide, and deciding means one of the two animals in front of you walks out having lost, and Roger cannot do it. He sees it from where they are standing. He sees it from where the other one is standing too, immediately and completely, and he sits there with both of them true at once and the room waiting. He has adjourned hearings to think about it for a week. He has found for both sides in writing, twice, which Ned had to file as two documents.

What the borough worked out, eventually, is the ha'penny. When a call is genuinely even Roger takes it out, and somebody else calls it in the air, and whatever it does is what happens, and Roger writes it down and everyone goes home. He has never once called it himself. He says that would be taking a side. The ha'penny is worn almost smooth now and it has settled four boundary questions, a dispute about a bandstand, and who was to have the good pitch at the fair, and the borough considers all four of those settled forever.
characters.voice: Mild, apologetic, extremely capable. Starts sentences with 'well, the thing is, from where he's sitting —'. Says 'that's fair' to both animals in the same conversation and means it both times.
characters.arc: Five rungs and one worn ha'penny. The Locksmith at 1 is the fixing, before anyone made an office of it — and even then a tie pays him. The Records Clerk at 2 is the borough's paperwork and the Fox's eye on the Capital City. The Circuit Judge at 3 is the first real bench, where a tie starts paying properly. The Fair Broker at 4 is the animal in the middle of a bidding war who can push his own side once the room has stalled. The Ombudsman at 5 is the whole of it: he wins the ties he cannot decide, and every one of them pays.

wantedArt.why: The Fair Broker is two traders and a fox between them with a coin in the air. neighbors/6 is the bench portrait and boroughs/2 is the lock bench; neither has the toss in it.
wantedArt.painted: Painted. mk_roger_fair_broker_4 → the neighbors atlas, tile 6. (A Maker atlas tile wins over anything on the card itself — `explicitArt` in src/ui/painted-art.js reads MAKER_ART_TILES first — so a card that still carries the older shared `art` shows the commissioned scene.)

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for chance: an effect that tosses Roger's ha'penny and does one thing on heads and another on tails — the borough's actual method for a call that will not come down on its own.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The one genuine coin toss the engine already has: the tied bid. `onTiedBid` fires exactly when two Mayors have put up the same number and neither is right, which is the situation Roger is for, and everything he does hangs off it. It is chance the players walked into rather than chance he can call on demand.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `coinFlip`: `{ heads, tails }`, each side an effect of its own. It draws on the same seeded rng every shuffle uses, so a game is still replayable from its seed and the toss goes in the log rather than hiding inside the effect. The Fair Broker tosses on a tied bid, which is still the situation he is for — but the ha'penny is a real one now, and somebody else calls it, exactly as his flavor always said.

characters.name: Earl
characters.backstory:
Earl keeps the tea house, which is not the café and never has been. Bean's counter by the Hiring Hall has the mornings and the accounts and the noise; Earl has the long afternoons, when an animal who needs to sit down with somebody for two hours comes and sits down with somebody for two hours. The two of them have never competed for an hour in their lives and Earl buys his leaf through Bean's supplier, which he will tell you is the only sensible arrangement in the borough.

There are two Earls and the difference between them is a pot of tea. The first one — the afternoon one, the one with a cup already poured — is the calmest animal in the First Boroughs. He listens for an hour without moving, says one thing at the end of it, and animals go away and act on the one thing. The second Earl is what is there before the first cup: fast, loud, four jobs at once, halfway up a ladder with the urn in one paw, talking through a plan that has three steps too many in it. That Earl gets an enormous amount done. That Earl also once reorganised the entire back room at four in the morning, on his own, and could not find anything in it for a fortnight.

What both Earls do is push animals up. He has a thing about it — he cannot watch somebody be good at a job and stay in it. Half the borough's apprentices have been talked into the next thing across his counter, usually over a pot they did not pay for, and when it is genuinely a coin-toss whether an animal is ready he will lean on it, hard, in favour of ready. He has been wrong perhaps four times. He counts them. He will tell you all four if you have an afternoon.
characters.voice: Two speeds and nothing in between. With tea: slow, warm, one sentence at a time. Without: three sentences at once, all of them started. Says 'right — next thing' at both speeds.
characters.arc: Four rungs of the same push, and the tea decides how hard. The Tea Boy at 0 hands a note over with the tray and the next upgrade costs less. The Tea Trader at 2 does it every shift. The Coffee Roaster at 3 is Earl off the tea entirely, frantic at the roaster at four in the morning — and when the room stalls on an even call, that is when he leans hardest. The Tea House Keeper at 4 is the afternoon at its best: he is back on the floor with a cup already poured, and the next animal you push up a rung comes cheap.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a favourable coin flip before Earl helps anybody upgrade: the toss is whether the animal is ready, and Earl leans on it.
wantedVerbs.workaround: The one genuine coin toss the engine already has: the tied bid. `onTiedBid` fires exactly when two Mayors have put up the same number and neither is right, which is the situation Roger is for, and everything he does hangs off it. It is chance the players walked into rather than chance he can call on demand.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built as `coinFlip`, the same verb Roger asked for. Earl leans on his where the story put it: the Coffee Roaster tosses when he finishes a shift, and heads is the favourable call — the upgrade rate — while tails is the Supply he would have made anyway. An even call about whether an animal is ready, settled the way the borough settles one.

characters.name: Sage
characters.backstory:
Sage learned to read on the Lending Library's low shelf, which is where the scientific romances live — the penny serials about the other side of the sky, rockets the shape of a thumb, animals on a red world who are polite and terrifying. They read the lot before they were ten and then read them again, and they have never entirely stopped. Everything Sage knows about the sky started as somebody's invention, and the fact that some of it turned out to be true is, they will tell you, the best thing that has ever happened to anybody.

So they took the dome. Sage keeps the borough's watch list — what is due, what is late, what has not been seen since a year nobody here was alive for — and they keep it to the minute. The Crown wanted to know when the comet would come and Sage told them to the minute and then went back to bed. Sota grinds the lenses and has no interest whatever in what they are pointed at; Sage is the opposite animal, and the two of them work the same bench for whole nights without either saying anything the other wants to hear.

And they will not go. The selection board has left the application form on Sage's desk three times, flat, unmentioned, the way you leave a thing for somebody who has said no politely. Sage knows the space division better than the space division does — they have read the manifests, they sit in on the launch meetings, they are the animal Comet writes to from the pad — and they have never once put a name on the form. It is very high up, they say, and there is no one to tell if something goes wrong, and anyway somebody has to be down here looking, or what is the point of anyone going.
characters.voice: Precise about numbers, hopeless about wonder — a forecast to the minute and then a sentence about what it would be like to stand there. Says "somebody has to be looking" the way other animals say sorry.
characters.arc: Three rungs and one dome. The Night Assistant at 0 reads ahead in the town's own deck. The Astronomer at 3 reads the Capital City too, because the sky and the market both come round on a schedule. The Royal Astronomer at 5 does all of it every morning and draws what comes of it: the watch list that the Crown pays for.

wantedVerbs.why: Sage's whole gift is knowing the order things arrive in; the story wanted them to put the Capital City's deck back in a chosen order the way `reorderDeckTop` does for a town's own deck. `peekMarketDeck` only looks.
wantedVerbs.workaround: They look at the Market Deck and reorder their own — the borough's side of the sky, which is the half Sage is allowed to touch.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `peekMarketDeck` takes `reorder`, and the look at the Capital City's deck ends with the watcher putting it back the way they want it. Sage's top rung carries it — the Royal Astronomer sets the order the Capital City deals in at the start of every turn — and so does the Star Party, where the whole borough is out on the hill looking at the same sky. The Astronomer at 3 still only looks, which is what makes the promotion mean something.

characters.name: Eric
characters.backstory:
Eric was six when he told his parents he was going to be a farmer. His parents are lawyers — Capital City lawyers, the kind the Counting House budgets for a year ahead — and the borough fully expected a row. There was no row. They took him at his word, the way they would take a client at their word, and then they did what that family does with a thing once it has been decided: they bought the best of it. The best agricultural schools. The county-fair circuit every summer from when he was nine. A shelf of seed catalogues that arrived in the post like briefs.

And then, because neither of them could bear to be the least informed animal in a room, they learned it alongside him. His mother can judge a fleece and has the rosettes to prove it. His father reads the almanac cover to cover the week it comes off Lynnette's press and argues with the planting tables in the margin. All three of them show at the county fair and all three of them are a nuisance to beat.

What Eric actually turned out to be good at is not growing things, though he grows things very well. It is knowing what an animal costs to keep for a season, to the Supply, and being willing to say so out loud in front of them. He hires cheaply and he hires well, and nobody has ever accused him of hiring meanly, because the figure he says out loud is the figure he pays and it is usually better than the one they were going to ask for. The borough's wage rates are compared against Eric's, and the grange has quietly stopped arguing with him about it.
characters.voice: Plain, unhurried, and full of numbers he is not showing off about. Says what a thing costs before he says whether he wants it. Calls his parents "the lawyers" with enormous affection.
characters.arc: Five rungs up a farm the lawyers paid for. The Smallholder at 1 knows one animal's keep and shaves it off the next hire. The Fair Steward at 2 learned the trick on the circuit, where you price everything. The Row Farmer at 3 is the Rabbit's own verb — he brings somebody along, and the next hire is cheaper for it. The Row Boss at 4 runs a rate every morning; the Best Farmer There Ever Was at 5 runs it at double, which is what the schooling was for.

wantedArt.why: The top of the arc is Eric and both lawyers in the ring at the county fair with the rosette. It carries boroughs/8, the Row Farmer's field, as a stand-in: nothing in any atlas shows the top of Eric's arc.

wantedVerbs.verb: a standing recruitDiscount that is not spent by the first recruit
wantedVerbs.why: The story wanted a rate — every animal you hire while Eric is standing there costs 1 less — because that is what "he knows what an animal costs to keep" means. `recruitDiscount` is consumed whole by the first recruit it applies to (`consumeModFor`), so it can only ever say "your next recruit".
wantedVerbs.workaround: A discount re-issued every turn: the Row Boss at 4 and the Best Farmer at 5 each hand one out at the start of your turn, so a Mayor who hires once a turn gets the rate and one who hires twice does not.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `townRecruitDiscount`, a passive carrying a value, read by `recruitCost` through `passiveTotal` and never spent by anybody. Eric's two top rungs are rates rather than re-issued discounts now — 1 less on every hire at the Row Boss, 2 at the Best Farmer There Ever Was — and they stop the moment he sits down, because a rate is a thing an animal is standing there saying. The cheap rungs keep their one-off discounts, so the arc reads discount, discount, rate.

characters.name: Benjamin
characters.backstory:
Benjamin makes the borough's lanterns, and he keeps the borough's fire record, and he has never been able to explain to anybody's satisfaction that these are the same job. Light shows us who we truly are, he says, which sounds like a lantern maker being poetic until you watch him do it: he will hold a lamp up to a beam and tell you the year the shed above it burned, who rebuilt it, what they rebuilt it out of, and why the joint is wrong.

The fire is the first half. He has been at it since he was small enough to be carried away from it — a wick, a dish of oil, the blue at the bottom of the flame, the exact moment a lamp catches. The borough has decided this is fine. It is fine because Benjamin is the most careful animal in the First Boroughs about it: he is the one who goes round the sheds in the dry weeks, he is the one who made Morty move the mill's spare oil, and the standing arrangement that the night round's lamps are filled at his bench and nowhere else is his own rule, not the ward's.

The second half is the record. Everything in this town that has ever burned is written down in Benjamin's hand, and because a fire record is really a record of what a place chose to rebuild, he ended up the animal the borough asks about its own history. He works the Town Dump the way other animals work a shelf — a thing thrown out is a thing somebody decided about, and he will go and get it back, and he is nearly always right that it was wanted. Mandee carries his lanterns on the night round, and between the two of them the night shift has never stumbled.
characters.voice: Warm, a little grand, and absolutely serious about light. Starts sentences with "The year that went —". Will not let you leave a lamp where he can see it is wrong.
characters.arc: Five rungs and one flame. The Wick Trimmer at 0 is the Otter keeping others moving. The Lantern Maker at 2 starts going back into the Dump, a card at a time, to the bottom of the deck. The Town Historian at 3 does both halves of his job in one shift — a shift moved, a thing recovered. The Master Lantern Maker at 4 gets it back into his hand instead, and the Keeper of the Light at 5 does it every morning, because by then the record is the town's and not his.

wantedArt.why: The Historian wants the fire book open on a trestle with a lamp held over a burnt beam. It carries neighbors/13, Benjamin's lamplighter portrait, as a stand-in — the right animal, the wrong hour.

wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a character who can return cards from the Town Dump. The engine only reaches Events there — `eventFromDumpToHand` and `eventFromDumpToDeckBottom` — and the one verb that reaches any card in a bin, `takeFromCityDump`, is the Raccoon's and works the shared City Dump instead. A Market card or a Character in your own Town Dump cannot be got back at all.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Events only, on four of the five rungs — which is the half of the Dump the engine can see. It is also, awkwardly, the Mouse's signature on an Otter, so Benjamin keeps `moveShift` and `readyNextTurn` on the rungs either side of it and reads as an Otter who happens to go through bins.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `cardFromDumpToHand`, which reaches any card of yours in the Town Dump rather than only the Events, with a `filter` for cards that should reach less far. The Master Lantern Maker takes back anything costing 3 or less; the Keeper of the Light takes back anything at all. The narrow verb stays the narrow verb and the two cheap rungs still use it, which is the arc: the bench, then the bin, then the whole record.

characters.name: Jessica
characters.backstory:
Jessica teaches the little ones, and she has never in her life set homework. The borough's parents raised this with her once, some years ago, in a meeting; Jessica agreed that homework was a very good idea and said she would think about it, and then went back and taught them the constellations as a round with actions. The kittens can name every one of them. Not one of them can spell any of them. The parents have stopped bringing it up.

The method is songs, games and activities, in that order, and it is not a softness — it is the only thing she has ever found that works on an animal who is convinced they are no good at this. She gets them singing the thing before they know it is the thing. By the time a kitten notices they are doing arithmetic they have been doing it for a fortnight and are annoyed about having been tricked, which Jessica regards as the moment the job is done.

She runs the night school as well, which is where the other half of her work happens, because the animals who turn up at the night school are not kittens. They are animals already doing a job who have worked out they would like to be doing a better one, and Jessica is the one who finds the next rung and talks them onto it before they have finished explaining why they could not possibly. Half the Hiring Hall's promotions in the last ten years started in that room. She is small, extremely loud, and has never once been to bed before four.
characters.voice: Delighted, fast, and slightly out of breath. Everything is an activity. Ends explanations with "— right, everybody up".
characters.arc: Four rungs and no homework. The Song and Game Leader at 0 is the Owl signature done literally: everybody up, on their feet, now. The Infant Teacher at 1 and the Night School Teacher at 2 start paying for the next rung — a promotion in your own town costs less. The Headmistress at 4 hands that rate out every morning, at double, which is what ten years of the night school actually amounts to.

wantedArt.why: The songs-and-games rung is a room of kittens on their feet doing the constellations as a round with actions. It carries nightworkers/3, the Headmistress at her desk, as a stand-in, which is the one thing Jessica is never doing.

characters.name: Jake
characters.backstory:
Jake came out from the Capital City with a reputation the Hiring Hall has never been given the details of, and has never asked for, because the one time somebody did ask he told them and they wished they had not. He is a warren runner: the long errands, the far rows, the sacks at the wrong end of the borough at the wrong end of the night. It is the job nobody wants and he is frankly wasted in it, and both of those things are the point.

He is down on his luck in the specific, cheerful way of an animal who has been down on his luck before and knows exactly how long it lasts. He does not borrow. He does not explain. He turns up at the grange, says what he will do it for, does about three animals' worth of it, takes the money in his paw rather than on the book, and then one morning the borough looks round and Jake is not there. He has done it twice. Nobody has an address for him. The road is the point — he talks about it the way Benjamin talks about light, which is to say constantly and without embarrassment.

The borough's older animals compare him to Kevin, and the comparison is wrong in the way that matters. Kevin stays a fortnight and every one of his eleven employers would have him back. Jake leaves before anybody has decided anything about him at all, which is a trick, and which is the same trick every time.
characters.voice: Quick, funny, slightly too familiar on the first morning. Never answers a question about where he was. Says "before I go" a lot, from the first day.
characters.arc: One rung, and it is a short one on purpose. Jake is hired out of the Capital City, works like three animals for two turns, and is on the road — the whole of him is the trade between what he earns you and how little of him you get to keep.

wantedVerbs.verb: a hire who can be re-hired after leaving
wantedVerbs.why: Jake has done it twice and the story wants the borough to be able to take him on again the next time he drifts through. A `leavesAfter` hire goes back to the Capital City and the card is simply out of the game for that Mayor.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Two turns, a big shift, and the Supply in his paw. The second visit is a story the flavor tells rather than a thing the engine does.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `returnsToMarket` on a card with `leavesAfter`. When the retainer is up Jake goes to the bottom of the Market Deck instead of the City Dump, so the next time the deck comes round to him either Mayor may take him on again. The card now says what the story always said — he leaves, and he turns up again — and `power.js` pays it as the chance it is rather than as a second term.

characters.name: Faustus
characters.backstory:
Faustus is the loudest animal in any room he is measuring, and he is usually measuring. He is a threadmaster of all types — cloth, canvas, cord, the awful modern stuff the Science hall sends over in sealed tins — and the trick everybody knows him for is that you do not bring him a drawing. You tell him what you want it to look like. You describe it, badly, waving, and he watches your paws rather than your face, and by the time you have finished the sentence he has the bolt down off the shelf and is cutting.

What that has made him, in a town that settles everything by auction, is a fixture of the auction room. Festival week, the regatta, the big lots at the Auction House: Faustus dresses the bidders, and he dresses them on the understanding that he will be in the room to see it. He has opinions about what a well-cut coat does to a bidding war and they are not modest opinions and they are, annoyingly, correct. A Mayor who turns up to the Capital City in something Faustus made has already cost everybody else a rung before anybody has said a number, and the Auction House has quietly stopped pretending otherwise.

He is a Cat, which means all of this happens exactly when it suits him and not a moment before, and he has walked out of a fitting because the light was wrong. Daisy does the flowers for festival week and Faustus does the coats, and the two of them have an arrangement about the square that neither will describe as a friendship.
characters.voice: Loud, delighted, endlessly specific about fabric. Interrupts. Calls everybody "darling" and means it about half the time.
characters.arc: Five rungs, all of them pointed at the auction room. The Bolt Boy at 0 is paid to be in the room when you announce. The Pressure-Suit Tailor at 1 makes a challenge cheaper; the Costumier at 2 makes it win ties. The Sailmaker at 3 is the Cat signature — he gets up when it suits him. The Threadmaster at 5 is the whole thing said out loud: while he is on display in the Capital City, every pledge in every auction costs a rung more, for everybody, and the Mayor who finally hires him gets the first bid of the turn as well.

wantedArt.why: The Threadmaster is a hire out of the Capital City, at the Auction House door in something he made this morning. It carries whiskerwood/3, the quilting bench, as a stand-in — the job he was promoted out of.

wantedVerbs.verb: a pledge rule that only binds the rival
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for a card that makes players spend two animals a bid while it is out. `pledgeLadderDelta` does exactly that, and it does it to both Mayors — including the one who hired him — because a `displayed` city rule is a rule of the room, not of a town.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Split across the same card: the ladder is heavier while Faustus sits in the Capital City, and once a Mayor buys him out of the room they get the first bid of each turn a rung higher instead. Buying him is buying the door, which is the shape Bob's gate already established.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `opponentPledgeLadderPlus1`, a passive that raises the OTHER Mayor's pledge ladder and not its owner's, alongside the Statue burdens that already reach across the table. The Threadmaster keeps the displayed rule, which is a rule of the room and falls on everybody in it; buying him out of the display turns it into a rule that falls on your rival alone. Buying him is still buying the door — it is simply narrow on the other side of you now.

characters.name: Thistle
characters.backstory:
Thistle works, and that is nearly the whole of what the borough can tell you about him. Up before the lanterns, home after the moon, thirty-odd years of it, and in all that time nobody has had a word out of him that was not about the job or worth hearing. He is not shy and he is not sullen. He simply does not see why a thing that can be done should be discussed first.

What he is actually for, the grange worked out early and has never said to his face: put Thistle at the head of a row and the row keeps his pace. Not because he drives it — he has never once looked back — but because the pace is exactly right, and an animal who falls in behind him comes off that field at dusk having done half again what they meant to and not feeling it until the morning. The grange sends him out with the ones who think they are no good. It works about nine times in ten, and the tenth is usually a fox.

And there is the other thing. Two evenings a month, in whatever room is having the open mic, there is a badger at the back by the door who does not take his coat off, does not drink anything, listens to one singer's set with his eyes shut, and is gone before the applause. Cassadee keeps the list and knows exactly which nights he comes, and has never mentioned it to him, and has twice moved that singer up the running order so he would not have to stay so late. The borough has decided, collectively and without discussion, that this is nobody's business. It is the only thing about Thistle anybody gossips about, and they do it very quietly.
characters.voice: Short. Answers the question asked. Long silences that are not uncomfortable unless you make them so. The most he has ever said at once was about drainage.
characters.arc: Five rungs at one pace. The Almanac Keeper at 1 is the Badger signature: the town braces and the weather goes over it. The Field Hand at 2 pays his own next shift better; the Grange Warden at 3 starts paying for everybody's. The Field Surveyor at 4 and the Grange Elder at 5 are the thing the grange actually worked out — while Thistle is standing there, every shift the town finishes is worth more, and at the top it is worth two more, which is thirty years of pace made into a rate.

characters.name: Tuppence
characters.backstory:
Tuppence comes out from the Capital City about once a month with a cart, and what is on the cart is the best hour in the borough. Nobody, including Tuppence, can always say what the things are. There is a brass object with a hinge. There is a crate of the ribbed glass that the Observatory later turned out to want very badly. There is a coil of something that Moss looked at for a long minute, bought the whole of, and used on a bridge arch, and which the Capital City's guild has since written to ask about.

The trade is not junk and it is not antiques. Tuppence buys ahead of the borough's understanding — the fittings, the stuff, the odd modern material that nobody here has a use for yet — and then waits, which is the most Squirrel thing about them and the reason they are never quite as poor as the cart looks. Half of what is screwed, hung, glazed or bolted into the First Boroughs' Buildings came off that cart at a price the Counting House still does not believe, and the standing joke at the Counting House is that Tuppence's invoices are cheaper than the queries about them.

They and Hazel have the obvious arrangement: what the day market cannot name goes to the night market, where not being able to name a thing is the whole appeal. Patch is the other end of it — animals bring Patch a thing and ask whether it is worth keeping, and about four times a year the thing turns out to have come off Tuppence's cart, and Patch says yes, and does not explain why.
characters.voice: Cheerful, vague about provenance, precise about price. "I don't know what it is either. It's four Supply, and you'll want two."
characters.arc: One rung, hired out of the Capital City, because the cart only ever comes out once a month. It does two things at once, which is the whole trade: a Building goes up cheaper while Tuppence is in town, and what they make on the shift goes under the cart rather than into the till.

characters.name: Velvet
characters.backstory:
Velvet is a government cat. His mother was a government cat and her mother kept the Capital City's tithe rolls, and Velvet has never once in his life wanted to be anything else, which the borough finds faintly alarming and Velvet finds restful. He came out to the First Boroughs as a petition runner at seventeen and has been behind one counter or another ever since.

What he holds now is the consents. Nothing goes up in this town and nothing comes down without a form Velvet has read aloud to somebody, slowly, all of it, while they fidget. Ned keeps the ward records and Velvet keeps the consents; they are different shelves and in fifteen years the two have never disagreed, which both of them regard as ordinary and everybody else regards as slightly eerie. Moss's formal warning from the Capital City came across Velvet's counter, and Velvet read that aloud too, at the same pace, to a badger who wanted to be anywhere else in the world.

The thing to understand about him is that he is not enduring any of this. He loves it. He loves the mundane — a well-ruled column, a fee scale that comes out even, a Tuesday. He loves patterns, and he sees them, which is why he is the animal who noticed the far hedgerow appearing in three unrelated files in one spring and said so before anybody else had. And he loves the queue: the small talk while a long form is filled in is, he has said in a public meeting, the best part of his week. The borough was startled, thought about it, and decided to believe him.
characters.voice: Unhurried, kind, faintly pleased. Reads things aloud in full. Asks after your aunt while the ink dries, and remembers the answer next quarter.
characters.arc: Five rungs and one counter, going from the form to the fabric of the town. The Counter Clerk at 1 gets one Building through cheaper. The Notary at 2 is the Cat signature: he gets up when the small print says he may. The Neighborhood Registrar at 3 runs the discount every morning. Then the other half of the office opens: the Surveyor of Works at 4 takes a Building down and puts a discarded one up in its place, and the Clerk of the Works at 5 does both — the rate and the demolition order — which is the whole consents shelf in one animal.

wantedArt.why: The Surveyor of Works is outdoors for once: a cat in a good coat with a clipboard, in front of something about to come down. It carries whiskerwood/4, the counter portrait, as a stand-in.

wantedVerbs.verb: buildingsAtLeast as a scaling condition on a discount
wantedVerbs.why: The story wanted the rate to read as an office that gets better at its own job — the more this town has raised, the cheaper the next consent. `buildingsAtLeast` exists as a yes/no condition, but nothing scales a mod's value by a count.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Two flat rates on two rungs: 1 less at the Registrar, 2 less at the Clerk of the Works. The office gets better because Velvet is promoted, not because the town got bigger.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: a mod's value may be counted rather than printed. `addMod` takes `valuePer: "buildingsBuilt"` and a `max`, so a rate can scale with what the town has actually raised. The Clerk of the Works is 1 off every Building and 1 more for each one already standing, up to 3 more: the office gets better at its own job, which is what the story asked for. The Registrar below him stays a flat rate, because he is a promotion away from the counting.

characters.name: Mandee
characters.backstory:
Mandee works nights. Only nights — the courier run, the weather watch on the dome, the trestles coming down at Hazel's market at four, the loads that go on the water when the water is empty. She is at the sorting bench before Hibiscus and gone before Juniper, she is on Taco's cart list, and she has never once been seen in the First Boroughs in daylight by an animal who could later produce a witness.

Nobody knows where she lives. This is not a figure of speech and the borough has tested it: Hoot keeps the list of animals who have asked to be woken and Mandee is not on it, the Hiring Hall has a line for an address and hers is blank, and twice now somebody has set out to walk with her at the end of a run and found, perfectly pleasantly, that they were walking home alone. The borough has two animals it does not ask about — Barnaby is the other — and has decided not to compare notes, which is itself a decision it made without discussing.

What she trades in, besides freight, is tales. They are very good tales. They are about the far bank and the long road and a thing at the county line in a bad winter, they are told at exactly the pace of a walk, and not one of them has ever been checked. Scott, who has Ned certify everything he prints about a real animal or a real year, keeps a whole shelf of Mandee's and files it with the invention, and has said, once, in a way that was not a joke, that he is not sure that is the right shelf.

And she is never slow. Whatever she is hired to be — the courier, the watcher, the trader with the good coat — Mandee arrives on her feet and ready to go, at an hour when everybody else is turning over.
characters.voice: Low, amused, unhurried. Answers a question with a story that is almost an answer. Says "I'll be off, then" while already off.
characters.arc: Four rungs and no daylight. The Night Courier at 1 is a Fox reading the Capital City one card ahead. From the Weather Watcher at 2 upward, every rung carries the same line — recruit, and somebody turns one step toward upright, and the animal she picks is usually herself, which is the promise the maker made about her. The Moonlight Trader at 3 adds the Fox's first bid; the Keeper of Tales at 4 makes the whole town's Masters arrive a turn nearer, which is Mandee's own habit finally spreading to everybody else.

wantedVerbs.verb: entersUpright (a card that sets its own entry orientation)
wantedVerbs.why: The maker asked for all of Mandee's variations to arrive ready, regardless of class. Entry orientation is read off the cost alone (`entryOrientation` in actions.js) before the animal is even on the table, so a card cannot change its own — the only two things that touch it, `masterDelayMinus1` and the Statue of Patience's burden, are player passives already in force when the recruit happens.
wantedVerbs.workaround: Three of them: an Apprentice rung, which arrives upright by the rules anyway; `onRecruit → advanceCharacter` on every rung above it, which the player spends on Mandee herself to stand her up the moment she lands; and `masterDelayMinus1` on the Keeper of Tales, so the next Master this town hires — Mandee included — comes in a turn nearer. An upgrade recruit keeps the stack's orientation, so once one Mandee is upright the rest of her arc genuinely does arrive ready. `advanceCharacter` is the Owl's signature and this is the one place a Fox borrows it; she keeps `peekMarketDeck` and `firstBidPlus1` so the auction animal is still the animal.
wantedVerbs.resolved: Built: `entersUpright` on a card. Entry orientation is otherwise read off the cost alone, before the animal is on the table; this is the one thing that can say otherwise, and it is read by the recruit action and by `recruitFromHand` alike, so she arrives ready however she got here. All four Mandees carry it. The Statue of Patience's burden still sits her down, because that is a rule of the town and this is only a fact about one animal — and the `onRecruit → advanceCharacter` workaround has come off the rungs that only had it to stand her up.

characters.name: Willow
characters.backstory:
Willow started with one ferry. She was nineteen, it was not a good ferry, and she talked the previous owner into terms that he described for years afterwards as generous of him. She now signs for everything that floats between the ferry steps and the county line, and for a good deal that does not: the boat yard, the two rows of cottages on the towpath, the lease on the arcade, the whole of the harbour office. She sells big. She has never in her life sold anybody a small thing, and the borough is not certain she knows how.

What she is, technically, is the Harbourmaster, which means the River Otter licence is granted out of her office, and the river trade's whole ladder — dock hand, ferry hand, lighterman, wright — runs up to a desk she sits behind. Brooke has been about two years off it for eight years and knows exactly whose desk that is. Willow is not unfair about it. She is simply the largest fact in that room, and she takes up all of it, and she talks.

The talking is the thing. She is the best talker in the First Boroughs and the borough is proud of her for it in the way you are proud of weather.
